  CITY OF SANTA MONICA

  CITY COUNCIL MINUTES

  APRIL 8, 2025

  A regular meeting of the Santa Monica City Council was called to order by Mayor Negrete at 5:31 p.m., on
  Tuesday, April 8, 2025, at City Council Chambers, 1685 Main Street, Santa Monica, California and a
  teleconference site at The Diplomat Beach Resort, 3555 S. Ocean Drive, Hollywood, Florida.

  Roll Call:  Present:  Mayor Lana Negrete
  Mayor Pro Tem Caroline Torosis
  Councilmember Jesse Zwick
  Councilmember Dan Hall (arrived remotely at 6:21 p.m.)
  Councilmember Ellis Raskin
  Councilmember Barry Snell
  Councilmember Natalya Zernitskaya

  City Attorney Douglas Sloan
  City Clerk Nikima S. Newsome

  CONVENE/PLEDGE  On order of the Mayor, the City Council convened at 5:31 p.m., with all
  members present except Councilmember Hall. Councilmember Raskin led
  the assemblage in the Pledge of Allegiance.

  STATEMENT OF  The City of Santa Monica is located on the land of Tovangaar. With
  ACCOUNTABILITY  great respect, the City acknowledges the Gabrieleño/Tongva as the First
  (LAND  People of this ancestral and unceded territory of Kuruvungna, a village
  ACKNOWLEDGEMENT)  that we know as Santa Monica. We honor their elders, past and present,
  and the Gabrieleño descendants who are part of the Gabrieleño /Tongva
  tribes.

  We recognize that these peoples are still here, and as settlers and kuyam
  (guests), we recognize our responsibility and obligation to care for their
  land in partnership with them. The City of Santa Monica commits to
  work in partnership with the Gabrieleño/Tongva people to uplift their
  voices and visibility on their ancestral land.

  The City of Santa Monica Statement of Accountability (Land
  Acknowledgement) was read into the record by Mayor Pro Tem Torosis.

  LEVINE ACT  Pursuant to the Levine Act (Govt Code Section 84308), any party to a
  DISCLOSURE  permit, license, contract, or other entitlement before the Council is
  required to disclose on the record any contribution, including

  ORDINANCES:  10.A. Introduction and First Reading of Ordinance Updating Public
  PUBLIC NUISANCE  Nuisance Abatement and Administrative Citation Codes, was presented.
  ABATEMENT AND
  ADMINISTRATIVE  Recommended Action
  CITATION CODES  Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Adopt a finding of no possibility of significant effect pursuant to
  Section 15061(b)(3) (Common Sense Exemption) of the California
  Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines; and
  2. Introduce for first reading an Ordinance amending the text of the
  Santa Monica Municipal Code by amending Chapter 13.06,
  Abatement of Nuisances, to add new classes of violations which may
  be deemed public nuisances, and amend Chapter 1.09.
  Administrative Citations, adding a new definition of responsible
  party, making clear the requirements for certain steps to be taken to
  align with Government Code 53069.4, defining required service
  procedures for administrative citations, and providing new incentives
  for violators to bring correctable violations into compliance.

  The City Attorney amended the ordinance on the floor as follows:

  Section 2 of the draft ordinance under the definition of “Responsible party”
  means any person, business, company or entity, and the parent or legal
  guardian of any person under the age of eighteen years, who has done any
  act for which an administrative citation may be imposed, should be stricken
  in the draft.

  Questions asked and answered of staff included: can the department
  accomplish all that is proposed in this ordinance with existing resources
  while also enforcing what is already on the books; has their been a good
  collaborative relationship with the City Attorney’s Office; are there
  additional resources needed from the City Attorney’s Office; is the City able
  to take as aggressive of action needed on any of the code cases that are
  referred for action; before these amendments was there no delegated
  authority to administer correctable citations; was this initiated at the request
  of Council as a result of calls for service ordinance; could it be a standard for
  vacant properties; how can persistent concerns be cataloged; how can it be
  ensured that persistent violators are escalated; could persistent violators be

  8  April 8, 2025
 Docusign Envelope ID: 900E3178-25A7-40CD-AE38-1F4E679CB055

  brought to the attention of Council; are sufficient deterrent measures being
  implemented; how are complaints triaged and prioritized; how can cases be
  better reported for tracking from open to close; is there any update from the
  CAO concerning leveraging penalties; are there metrics to determine areas
  of success and what are the key indicators; how is animal neglect being
  defined; are there escalating late fees on citations; do uncollected fines get
  sent to collections; would this apply to landlords who have violations at
  multiple locations; how is it being ensured that residents are being protected
  or getting assistance when relocation is necessary; is the City able to recover
  payment from illegal home shares; why did it take so long to handle the
  issues at the Pavillion Motel; would it be beneficial to put Code Enforcement
  under the CAO; are chronic nuisances being prioritized; is there a prohibition
  from a property owner or the owner’s designee imposing a penalty on a
  tenant; and when does Code Enforcement handle nuisance calls concerning
  alcohol use outside of businesses.

  Considerable discussion ensued on topics including, but not limited to
  kudos to Code Enforcement and Building and Safety; concerns about
  having the necessary resources to ensure these amendments can be
  implemented and enforced; three categories of concern in ensuring the laws
  are upheld including enforcement, record keeping, and manners and
  methods by which cases are escalated for additional intervention; legal
  constraints when it comes to specific standards to declare properties a
  nuisance or otherwise; concerns about citations being sent to collection
  agencies and potentially impacting the credit ratings of lower income
  residents; concerns about particular buildings in the city with obvious code
  enforcement issues that have not been addressed in many years; and noting
  that historically anti-loitering laws were used to unfairly target members of
  marginalized communities and ensuring that does not occur with the
  addition of anti-loitering measures in this ordinance.

  Direction was provided to staff to collaborate with the Rent Control Board
  with implementation.
